name: Midir

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Midir, called the proud, was an Irish fairy king and god. He plays a leading part in one of the most romantic tales of ancient Ireland. Midir fell in love with the beautiful Étain. He was already married to the jealous druid Fuamnach, who cast a spell on her rival. Étain became a fly, a beautiful fly. In that form she drowned in a glass of wine. A princess drank the wine and became pregnant. Her child was the reborn Étain, who married the king of Tara, Eochaid Airem. Midir still loved her. He came to Tara and set a riddle game, fidchell, with a kiss from Étain as the prize. As he kissed her, memory returned to Étain. Together they flew away through the skylight of Tara, joined by a golden chain. Midir also appears in the tale of the Tuatha Dé Danann. When the Dagda stepped down, the gods chose Bodb Derg to lead them. Midir alone refused to accept the choice and went to war. He did not win, and the bloodshed made the gods leave the surface of the world and hide in their sídhe palaces. Midir then lived in his own sídhe, Brí Léith, also called Slieve Callory or Ardagh Hill, in the west of County Longford. In local folklore he survives as Midas, a giant who steals children who pass his hidden palace.
